title: Functions
intro: Parameters always have types. The return type comes after `->`. The last line, written without a semicolon, is the return value.

coming_from.go: Types come after names like Go, with `-> i32` for the return type. The last expression without a semicolon is the return value, and `return` is still there for leaving early.
coming_from.kotlin: The shape is Kotlin's `fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int`, with `->` before the return type. Braces are always required (there is no `= a + b` body), and the last expression without a semicolon is the result, so `return` is only for leaving early.
coming_from.python: Like a fully type-hinted `def`, except the compiler enforces the hints and you must write them for every parameter. The last expression without a semicolon is returned, so leaving out `return` doesn't give you `None`.
coming_from.typescript: Same shape as `function add(a: number, b: number): number`, with `->` before the return type. Parameter types must always be written, and so must any return type other than nothing. The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.
coming_from.java: The return type goes after `->`, and the last expression without a semicolon is the return value, so `return` is only needed for early exits. Rust has no overloading, so two functions need two different names.
coming_from.csharp: The return type comes after `->`, and a block's last expression (no semicolon) is its result. Unlike an expression-bodied `=>` member, the block can hold statements first. Rust has no method overloading and no default or named arguments.
coming_from.c: `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32` is `int add(int a, int b)` with the return type moved to the end. The last expression without a semicolon is returned, and falling off the end of a function that should return a value is a compile error, not junk.
coming_from.cpp: The trailing `-> i32` is like C++'s trailing return type, and the last expression without `;` is the return value. Forgetting to return a value is a compile error rather than undefined behaviour, and Rust has no overloading or default arguments.

notes: `return a + b;` also works. The no-semicolon style is just shorter, and it is what most Rust code uses.
`&str` is the type for text you only read; a string literal such as `"kotlin"` has it. [Strings](/learn/strings/) comes later.
Functions can be declared after they are used. Their order in the file doesn't matter.

Arguments are passed by value, and a `String` passed in is moved, not copied ([Ownership](/learn/ownership/)). There are no default or named arguments and no overloading ([What Rust lacks](/learn/what-rust-lacks/)).

gotcha.title: A semicolon on the last line
gotcha.looks_fine: Go, Kotlin, Java and C# need an explicit `return`, so a stray semicolon changes nothing.
gotcha.rust_sees: In Rust a block's value is its last expression. Adding `;` turns `a + b` into a statement that produces nothing, written `()` and called the unit type.
gotcha.why: So the function now promises an `i32` and gives back `()`. The compiler's `help:` line points at the exact semicolon to remove.

go.says: Go refuses this too: `a + b` is "not used" and the function has a `missing return`. Go always needs an explicit `return`, so a stray semicolon can't change what a function returns.
go.error:
# command-line-arguments
./main.go:6:2: a + b (value of type int) is not used
./main.go:7:1: missing return

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too: a block body needs `return`, so a body whose last line is just `a + b` gives `missing return statement`.

python.says: Python prints None. Without `return`, the last line is worked out and thrown away, and the function gives back None.

typescript.says: TypeScript refuses this too: `add` promises a `number` but has no `return`. Without the `: number` it would compile and quietly return `undefined`.
typescript.error: main.ts(1,37): error TS2355: A function whose declared type is neither 'undefined', 'void', nor 'any' must return a value.

java.says: Java refuses this too: `a + b;` is "not a statement". Java always needs an explicit `return`, so a stray semicolon can't change what a method returns.
java.error:
Main.java:3: error: not a statement
        a + b;
          ^
1 error

csharp.says: C# refuses this too: `a + b;` is not a valid statement on its own, and the method never returns a value (CS0201, CS0161). C# always needs an explicit `return`.
csharp.error:
Program.cs(5,5): error CS0201: Only assignment, call, increment, decrement, await, and new object expressions can be used as a statement
Program.cs(3,12): error CS0161: 'Add(int, int)': not all code paths return a value

c.says: gcc only warns that `a + b` does nothing and that `add` never returns. The program prints 2 instead of 5: whatever value happened to be left behind. Another compiler or machine can print something else.
c.warnings:
main.c: In function ‘add’:
main.c:4:7: warning: statement with no effect [-Wunused-value]
    4 |     a + b;
      |     ~~^~~
main.c:5:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function [-Wreturn-type]
    5 | }
      | ^

cpp.says: g++ warns that `a + b;` does nothing and that `add` never returns, then builds it anyway. Running off the end is undefined behaviour, and here g++ plants a trap so the program dies before printing. On ARM, this site's machine, that is a trap signal (SIGTRAP); on x86 it is an illegal-instruction signal (SIGILL).

main.cpp: In function ‘int add(int, int)’:
main.cpp:4:7: warning: statement has no effect [-Wunused-value]
    4 |     a + b;
      |     ~~^~~
main.cpp:5:1: warning: no return statement in function returning non-void [-Wreturn-type]
    5 | }
      | ^
